newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate mulling immunity for donor Johnnie Chung.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate mulling immunity for donor Johnnie Chung.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Senate attorneys are negotiating with Taiwanese-American entrepreneur Johnny Chung, a central figure in the campaign fund raising investigation, on granting him immunity from prosecution in exchange for his testimony, Senate sources said.

One senior source who asked not to be named told Reuters: "Chung is asking for immunity. It's under consideration. We are in discussions with his lawyer. He's providing information of what he might testify to."

Testimony from Chung could be highly embarrassing for President Bill Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton. However, the Senate source said it appeared it would be difficult to reach an agreement.
"There are negotiations but I'm not optimistic they are going anywhere," he said.

The Senate Government Affairs Committee is investigating possible illegal or improper fund raising in the 1996 election campaign, with particular emphasis on the role of foreign money from Asian business interests.

Even if agreement with Chung were reached, it would likely face strong opposition from the Justice Department, which is conducting a criminal investigation into campaign fund raising. An immunity deal would also require the support of at least two Democrats on the committee.

Chung, a Taiwanese-born fax company operator turned international businessman, gave $366,000 to the Democratic National Committee between 1994 and 1996. The DNC returned all the money earlier this year because it suspected it may have come illegally from foreign sources.

After four weeks of testimony, the committee has adjourned for the summer recess. Hearings are expected to resume Sept. 2 and continue through December, when the committee is supposed to conclude its work.
Several key figures in the fund-raising scandal have either fled the country or refused to testify by asserting their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.
The Senate source said some of these might be summoned to appear before the committee in person so that the nation could see them refuse to answer questions.
"The notion that all you have to do is sit in an easy chair and send a form letter that you are not going to testify is not necessarily the way it is going to end up happening," the source said.
The sources said the hearings would likely resume with testimony about a Democratic fund-raising event at a Buddhist Temple outside Los Angeles in April 1996 attended by Vice President Al Gore.

Also likely to be called to testify in coming weeks were former DNC chairman Don Fowler and former senior Clinton adviser Harold Ickes. Committee lawyers were also likely to interview Connecticut Sen. Chris Dodd, who served alongside Fowler as chairman of the DNC but was less in touch with the day-to-day management of the party.

Chung gave a taste of what he might testify to in a Los Angeles Times interview last month in which he described how he handed a $50,000 check to Mrs. Clinton's then chief of staff Maggie Williams on White House grounds in March 1995.

Chung said he was trying to gain VIP treatment for a group of visiting Chinese businessmen and was given to understand by aides of Mrs. Clinton that access to the president and first lady would be forthcoming in exchange for a hefty donation.
Soliciting funds is illegal under the Hatch Act which prohibits federal employees from raising or receiving political contributions on federal property.

White House officials have acknowledged that Williams was given a check by Chung and arranged a meeting with Mrs. Clinton for the Chinese delegation. The group also got to see President Clinton deliver his weekly radio address and posed for pictures with the president.
The White House officials deny soliciting the contribution or providing favors in exchange for the donation.
